modules.title: The Science of Baking: Ratios, Ingredients and Heat
modules.overview: Professional bakers do not follow recipes blindly: they understand what each ingredient does and they work in weights and ratios. This module teaches baker's percentages, gluten control, the jobs of fat, eggs and sugar, how to choose and measure leaveners, and how to make an ordinary home or gas oven bake predictably.

lessons.title: Flour, gluten and baker's percentages
objectives: Choose the right flour for bread, cakes and pastry by its protein content
Control how much gluten develops by changing water, mixing and fat
Write any recipe in baker's percentages with flour as 100%
Scale a formula up or down accurately using percentages

blocks.text: Wheat flour contains two proteins, **glutenin** and **gliadin**. On their own they do nothing. When you add water and then mix or knead, they link together into a stretchy, elastic network called **gluten**. Gluten traps gas, so it is the skeleton of bread. In cakes and pastry, too much gluten makes the result tough, chewy or shrunken. Every advanced baker therefore asks one question first: how much gluten do I want in this product?

blocks.name: baguette-bread
blocks.caption: A chewy, open bread like this needs strong flour and well developed gluten.

blocks.text: Read the protein figure on the bag

The amount of gluten a flour can form depends mostly on its protein content. Nigerian flour bags list nutrition per 100 g; look for the protein line. Mills sell flour for bread, for confectionery and for general use, and the protein figure tells you which job it suits. The ranges below are the usual international guide.

head: Flour type
Typical protein
Best for
Why
rows: Builds strong gluten that holds gas and gives chew
Shortcrust, rough puff, choux, many cakes
A middle path: some strength, still tender
Weak gluten gives a fine, tender crumb

blocks.title: No cake flour in your market?
blocks.text: Make a close substitute: for every 100 g of all-purpose flour, remove 12 g and replace it with 12 g of cornflour (corn starch), then sift twice. The starch dilutes the protein, so less gluten forms.
Four levers that control gluten

items: **Water:** gluten cannot form without it. Less water (as in shortcrust) means less gluten.
**Mixing time:** kneading builds gluten; for cakes you mix flour only until it disappears.
**Fat:** fat coats flour proteins and blocks them from joining. This is literally where the word shortening comes from: fat shortens gluten strands.
**Sugar and acid:** sugar holds on to water, so less is available for gluten; acids such as buttermilk also tenderise.

blocks.title: How gluten forms
items: Glutenin and gliadin in flour
Add water
Mix or knead
Elastic gluten network
Traps gas, gives structure
blocks.caption: Remove water or mixing at any step and less gluten forms, which is what you want for tender cakes and pastry.

blocks.text: Baker's percentages: the professional language

In a bakery, recipes are called **formulas** and are written in baker's percentages. The total flour weight is always 100%. Every other ingredient is shown as a percentage of the flour, not of the whole dough. So a bread dough with 65% water uses 65 g of water for every 100 g of flour. This makes it very easy to compare recipes, spot a mistake, and scale up for a big order.

items: Weigh every ingredient in grams (cups and spoons vary too much for professional work).
Divide each ingredient's weight by the flour weight.
Multiply by 100 to get the percentage.
To scale, multiply the new flour weight by each percentage and divide by 100.

blocks.title: Worked example: converting and scaling a soft roll formula
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi bakes dinner rolls in Enugu. Her test batch uses 500 g flour, 300 g water, 10 g salt, 5 g instant yeast, 40 g sugar and 30 g butter. A caterer orders a batch three times bigger.
steps: Water: 300 divided by 500 = 0.60, so 60%.
New flour weight for three batches: 500 x 3 = 1,500 g.
Water: 1,500 x 60 / 100 = 900 g. Salt: 1,500 x 2% = 30 g. Yeast: 15 g. Sugar: 120 g. Butter: 90 g.
Check the total dough: 1,500 + 900 + 30 + 15 + 120 + 90 = 2,655 g. If each roll is 60 g, that is 2,655 / 60 = 44 rolls, with 15 g left over.
blocks.result: Ngozi's formula is 100% flour, 60% water, 2% salt, 1% yeast, 8% sugar, 6% butter. She can now scale to any order size in under a minute and know exactly how many rolls she will get.

blocks.text: Notice that salt at around 2% and instant yeast at around 1% are normal for bread. If a formula you find online shows 6% salt, you will now spot the error before you waste a bag of flour. Hydration, the water percentage, also tells you how the dough will feel: about 55 to 60% is firm and easy to shape, 65 to 70% is soft and slightly sticky, and above 75% is a wet dough that needs special handling.

blocks.title: Weigh, do not scoop
blocks.text: One cup of flour can weigh anywhere from about 120 g to 150 g depending on how it is scooped. A digital kitchen scale that reads in 1 g steps is the single most important tool for this course.

takeaways: Gluten forms when flour proteins meet water and are mixed.
Choose flour by protein: high for bread, low for soft cakes.
Water, mixing, fat and sugar are your four gluten controls.
Baker's percentages put flour at 100% and make scaling simple.

activity.title: Convert three recipes to baker's percentages
steps: Pick three recipes you use often: one bread, one cake, one pastry.
Convert every quantity to grams using your scale.
Work out each ingredient as a percentage of the flour weight.
Compare the water (or liquid) percentages of the three and note what that tells you about texture.
Scale the bread formula to 2 kg of flour.
activity.evidence: A notebook page or spreadsheet photo showing the three formulas in grams and percentages, plus the scaled bread formula.

lessons.title: What fats, eggs and sugar really do
objectives: Explain how fat tenderises, aerates and flakes depending on how it is used
Describe the structural and emulsifying jobs of egg whites and yolks
List at least four jobs of sugar beyond sweetness
Predict what happens when you cut sugar or swap butter for oil

blocks.text: Beginners think of butter, eggs and sugar as flavour. Professionals see them as **structure builders** and **tenderisers** working against each other. Flour and eggs build structure. Fat and sugar tenderise. A good formula balances the two sides. When a cake collapses, crumbles or turns rubbery, the balance is usually wrong.

blocks.name: butter
blocks.caption: Butter can tenderise, trap air or create flaky layers, depending on its temperature and how you mix it.

blocks.text: Fat: three jobs, three temperatures

head: How fat is used
Fat state
Result
Product
rows: Rubbed into flour in small pieces
Tiny air pockets that leaveners enlarge
Left in flat sheets between dough layers
Moist, soft crumb that stays soft when cool

blocks.text: Butter is not pure fat. It is roughly 80% fat with most of the rest water, and that water turns to steam in the oven, which helps puff pastry rise. Margarines and baking fats vary widely, so read the label. Oil is 100% fat and stays liquid when cool, which is why oil cakes feel moister the next day than butter cakes, even though butter tastes richer.

blocks.title: Heat is the enemy of creaming
blocks.text: In a hot Nigerian kitchen butter can turn greasy before you finish mixing. If the butter looks shiny and oily, it can no longer hold air. Chill it for 10 minutes, mix in the coolest part of the day, and stand the bowl in a tray of cool water if needed.
Eggs: builders, binders and emulsifiers

A large egg without its shell weighs about 50 g, and roughly three quarters of that is water. **Egg whites** are mostly water and protein. When whisked they trap air, and in the oven the proteins set, so they hold up sponges and meringues. **Yolks** contain fat and **lecithin**, a natural emulsifier that helps water and fat stay mixed. That is why a curdled cake batter often comes back together when you add a little flour, and why yolks make custards smooth.

items: Too few eggs: weak structure, the cake sinks or crumbles.
Too many eggs: rubbery, dry, eggy smell.
Cold eggs added to creamed butter: the fat hardens and the batter curdles. Use eggs at room temperature.

blocks.text: Sugar does much more than sweeten

items: **Tenderises:** it holds water, leaving less for gluten, and delays egg proteins from setting.
**Aerates:** sharp sugar crystals cut air pockets into butter during creaming.
**Keeps cakes moist:** sugar attracts moisture, so it slows staling.
**Browns:** sugar caramelises and takes part in the Maillard reaction, giving colour and flavour.
**Feeds yeast:** a little sugar speeds fermentation; a lot (above about 10% of flour) slows it.

blocks.title: Structure versus tenderness
items: Builders (toughen)
Tenderisers (soften)
blocks.caption: Change one side and you must think about the other, or the texture will shift.

blocks.title: Worked example: cutting sugar without ruining a cake
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna has a customer who wants a less sweet vanilla butter cake. Her formula is 250 g flour, 250 g sugar, 250 g butter, 250 g egg (about 5 eggs) and 125 g milk.
steps: She cuts sugar by 20%: 250 x 0.8 = 200 g. That removes 50 g of a tenderiser.
Because sugar also kept the cake moist, she adds 25 g more milk (125 + 25 = 150 g) to replace some lost moisture.
Less sugar means less browning, so she checks the cake 3 to 5 minutes earlier and relies on the skewer test, not colour.
She notes that with less sugar the cake will stale faster, so she tells the customer to eat it within two days or refrigerate it.
blocks.result: The cake is noticeably less sweet but still tender and moist. Halima records the new version as a separate formula: 100% flour, 80% sugar, 100% butter, 100% egg, 60% milk.

blocks.text: Big cuts, beyond about a quarter of the sugar, usually change the texture too much. For a truly low-sugar product it is better to choose a recipe designed for it than to keep cutting a classic one.
Swapping ingredients safely

items: **Butter to oil:** use about 80 g of oil for every 100 g of butter (butter is about 80% fat), and switch to a method that does not rely on creaming, because oil cannot hold air.
**Granulated sugar to brown sugar:** brown sugar carries molasses, which is acidic and moist; expect a softer, darker, slightly denser cake.
**Whole eggs to extra yolks:** a richer, more tender, more yellow crumb, but less lift and structure.
**Milk to water:** paler crust, because milk sugars and proteins help browning, and a slightly less tender crumb.

takeaways: Flour and eggs build; fat and sugar tenderise.
Fat temperature decides whether you get crumbly, airy or flaky results.
Yolks emulsify; whites trap air and set into structure.
Sugar also aerates, moistens, browns and feeds yeast.

activity.title: The butter versus oil test
steps: Bake two small loaf cakes from the same formula: one with butter, one with the same weight of vegetable oil.
Label them clearly and cool both completely.
Taste and press both on day one and again on day two.
Write down differences in flavour, softness and moisture.
activity.evidence: A photo of both cakes cut side by side and a short note of your day-one and day-two observations.

lessons.title: Leavening: air, steam, baking powder, soda and yeast
objectives: Name the three ways baked goods rise: air, steam and carbon dioxide
Choose between baking soda and baking powder for a given recipe
Calculate a sensible amount of chemical leavener for a batch
Recognise the signs of too much or too little leavening

blocks.text: Nothing rises unless gas expands inside it. There are only three sources of that gas: **air** you beat in, **steam** made from water in the oven, and **carbon dioxide** made by chemical leaveners or yeast. Almost every product uses more than one. A Victoria sponge uses creamed-in air plus baking powder. Choux pastry uses only steam. Bread uses carbon dioxide from yeast, plus steam in the first minutes of baking.

blocks.name: cupcake
blocks.caption: A good dome on a cupcake comes from air, steam and carbon dioxide working together.

blocks.title: Three sources of lift
items: Yeast or chemical CO2
Steam from water
Air beaten in
blocks.caption: Air is the base: leaveners only enlarge the bubbles you already created by creaming or whisking.

blocks.text: Baking soda and baking powder

**Baking soda** is sodium bicarbonate. It needs an acid to release carbon dioxide: buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon juice, brown sugar, natural cocoa or honey. Without enough acid, leftover soda tastes soapy and metallic and turns the crumb yellowish. Soda reacts as soon as it is wet, so batters made with soda only should go into the oven quickly.

**Baking powder** is soda already mixed with dry acid salts and a little starch to keep it dry. Most baking powder sold today is **double acting**: some gas is released when it gets wet, and more when it gets hot in the oven. That makes it forgiving if your batter waits a few minutes while you fill several tins.

head: Leavener
Needs
Typical amount
Watch out
rows: About 4 to 5 g (1 level tsp) per 125 g flour in cakes
Old powder loses strength; test it
About 1 g (a quarter tsp) per 125 g flour
Soapy taste if there is not enough acid
Soda neutralises the acid, powder gives the main lift
Common in buttermilk and chocolate cakes
Do not add the full amount again

blocks.title: Freshness test
blocks.text: Baking powder: stir half a teaspoon into a little hot water; it should fizz strongly. Baking soda: add a few drops of vinegar or lemon juice; it should bubble at once. Store both tightly closed, because humid air slowly uses them up.
More is not better

Too much chemical leavener makes bubbles grow so big that they join, rise to the top and burst. The cake rises fast, then sinks in the middle, with a coarse crumb and a bitter or salty taste. Too little gives a dense, heavy, tight crumb. If a formula seems wrong, compare it with the guide amounts above.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking the leavener in a buttermilk cake
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Ibadan found a red velvet recipe online for a 750 g flour batch. It lists 6 tsp baking powder and 3 tsp baking soda, and her trial cakes sank and tasted bitter.
steps: Guide for baking powder alone: 750 / 125 = 6 portions, so about 6 level tsp if powder were the only leavener.
But the recipe also has soda. Guide for soda: about a quarter tsp per 125 g, so 6 x 0.25 = 1.5 tsp.
The recipe has 3 tsp soda, double the guide, plus a full dose of powder. That is far too much total lift and too much soda for the acid in 500 ml buttermilk.
She reduces to 1.5 tsp soda and 3 tsp baking powder, keeping the buttermilk the same.
Second trial: level tops, fine red crumb, no bitter taste.
blocks.result: By checking each leavener against a guide amount, Bisi found the error and fixed it in one trial instead of five.

blocks.text: Steam and yeast in brief

Water turns to steam at 100 C and expands to well over a thousand times its volume. A very hot oven turns water in choux paste and in butter layers into steam fast, so they puff. Yeast is a living fungus that eats sugars and releases carbon dioxide and alcohol; it works slowly and also creates flavour. Module 4 covers yeast in depth.

Steam needs heat fast. That is why choux and puff pastry are baked hot, usually around 200 to 220 C, and why opening the oven door in the first 15 minutes can make them collapse: the burst of cool air stops steam production before the structure has set. For the same reason, a cake batter should not wait long at room temperature in a hot kitchen. Gas starts escaping, and the cake bakes flatter. Fill tins, level them, tap each tin once on the table to release large air pockets, and get them into a fully preheated oven.

blocks.title: Keep leaveners away from children
blocks.text: Baking soda and baking powder look like sugar or salt. Store them in labelled, closed containers on a high shelf, away from children and away from your salt.

takeaways: All lift comes from air, steam or carbon dioxide.
Soda needs an acid; baking powder carries its own.
Guide: about 1 tsp powder or a quarter tsp soda per 125 g flour.
Too much leavener makes cakes sink and taste bitter.

activity.title: Audit your leaveners
steps: Test the freshness of the baking powder and soda you have now.
Take two of your cake recipes and calculate the guide amount of leavener for their flour weight.
Compare with what the recipes actually use and mark any that look too high or too low.
Bake one adjusted recipe and note the result.
activity.evidence: A short note with your freshness test results, your calculations, and a photo of the adjusted cake's crumb.

lessons.title: Mastering your oven: calibration, heat and doneness
objectives: Check your oven's real temperature with an oven thermometer
Map hot spots and position trays for even baking
Adjust temperatures for fan ovens, dark tins and large cakes
Judge doneness by tests, not only by time

blocks.text: The same formula can come out perfect in one oven and burnt in another. Many home and small gas ovens in Nigeria have no accurate thermostat, and some only have a dial marked low, medium and high. A professional does not trust the dial. She measures, makes notes, and adjusts.

blocks.name: thermometer
blocks.caption: A cheap oven thermometer tells you the truth your oven dial may hide.

blocks.text: Step one: calibrate

items: Buy an oven thermometer (a small metal dial type that stands or hangs on the rack).
Place it in the centre of the middle shelf.
Set the oven to 180 C (or the mark you normally use for cakes) and wait at least 20 minutes.
Read the thermometer without opening the door for long. Note the real temperature.
Repeat at 160 C and 200 C, and write the three results on a card taped near the oven.

blocks.text: If the dial says 180 C but the thermometer reads 200 C, your oven runs 20 degrees hot, and you set the dial to about 160 C to get a true 180 C. Recheck every few months, and always after a repair or a new gas regulator.
Step two: map the hot spots

Almost every oven is hotter in some places. To find them, spread slices of plain white bread across a tray, bake at 180 C for a few minutes, and look at which slices toast first. Darker slices show hot spots, usually at the back or near the flame in gas ovens. Bake on the middle shelf, leave at least 3 to 5 cm of space between tins and the walls so hot air can move, and turn trays front to back about two thirds of the way through baking (never in the first half of a cake's bake, while it is still setting).

blocks.title: The oven control loop
items: Measure real temperature
Bake a test product
Record time and result
Adjust dial or position
Bake again
blocks.caption: Each round of testing makes your notes more reliable until your oven behaves predictably.

blocks.text: Adjusting for your equipment

head: Situation
What happens
Adjustment
rows: Lower the temperature by about 20 C, or check earlier
Lower by about 10 C, or use lighter tins
Lower by about 10 C and allow extra time
Cake deeper than about 8 cm or wider than 25 cm
Edges set long before the centre
Lower to about 160 C, bake longer, use a heating core or baking strips
Swap shelves partway and allow a few extra minutes

blocks.title: Gas oven safety
blocks.text: Light a gas oven exactly as the maker instructs, with the door open. If you smell gas, turn off the gas at the cylinder, do not light anything or switch on lights, open windows and doors, and get the leak checked before using the oven again. Keep a fire blanket or a suitable fire extinguisher in the kitchen, and use thick, dry oven gloves: a damp cloth transfers heat and can burn you.
Step three: judge doneness properly

items: **Cakes:** a thin skewer in the centre comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs; the top springs back when pressed lightly; the sides begin to pull away from the tin.

**Bread:** a deep, even crust colour and a hollow sound when tapped underneath. A probe thermometer in the centre is more reliable: lean bread is done at roughly 93 to 99 C, enriched bread at roughly 88 to 90 C.
**Pastry:** golden all over including the base. Pale pastry is undercooked and will turn soft.
**Choux:** deep golden and dry; if pale, the shells collapse when they cool.

blocks.title: Worked example: building an oven card
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Port Harcourt has a gas cooker with an oven dial marked 1 to 8 and no temperatures. Her cakes burn at the base.
steps: She tests with an oven thermometer after 20 minutes on each setting: mark 3 reads 155 C, mark 4 reads 175 C, mark 5 reads 200 C, mark 6 reads 225 C.
Her sponges need 180 C, so she uses mark 4 and adds about 5 C by placing the cake on the middle shelf, which tested slightly hotter.
The bread test shows the base burner area runs hot, so she places an empty baking tray on the shelf below the cake as a heat shield.
She bakes a test sponge: done in 24 minutes, skewer clean, base light golden.
She writes the card: Cakes 180 C = mark 4, middle shelf, tray shield below. Bread 220 C = mark 6. Pastry 200 C = mark 5.
blocks.result: With one afternoon of testing Grace stopped burning cake bases and now quotes reliable bake times when planning orders.

takeaways: Trust an oven thermometer, not the dial.
Map hot spots and give tins space for air to move.
Lower about 20 C for fan ovens and about 10 C for dark tins.
Use skewer, spring-back and internal temperature tests for doneness.

activity.title: Make your oven card
steps: Measure your oven's real temperature at three settings with an oven thermometer.
Do the bread-slice hot spot test and sketch where the hot spots are.
Bake one plain sponge and record shelf, setting, time and doneness test result.
Write a small oven card with settings for cakes, bread and pastry and tape it near your oven.
activity.evidence: A photo of your finished oven card and your hot spot sketch.

quiz.q: Funmi wants a very soft, fine chiffon cake. Which flour should she choose?
options: Cake or soft flour with about 8% protein
Any flour, because protein only matters for bread
quiz.explain: Low-protein flour forms less gluten, which gives the tender, fine crumb a chiffon cake needs.

quiz.q: A dough has 800 g flour and 520 g water. What is its hydration in baker's percentages?
quiz.explain: 520 divided by 800 = 0.65, so 65% hydration. Flour is always 100%.

quiz.q: Why does creaming fail when butter becomes shiny and greasy in a hot kitchen?
options: Melted butter cannot hold air pockets
quiz.explain: Creaming works by sugar crystals cutting air pockets into firm, soft butter. Once the fat is melted it cannot hold those pockets.

quiz.q: A cake recipe uses only baking soda but no buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon, cocoa or other acid. What is the likely result?
options: Poor rise and a soapy, metallic taste
quiz.explain: Soda needs an acid to react fully. Without it, the cake rises poorly and leftover soda tastes soapy.

quiz.q: Kemi's cakes rise fast then sink in the centre with a coarse crumb and bitter taste. What is the most likely cause?
options: Oven too cold for the first five minutes only
quiz.explain: Excess leavener makes bubbles grow, join and burst, so the cake collapses and tastes bitter.

quiz.q: Her oven thermometer shows 200 C when the dial is set to 180 C. To bake at a true 180 C she should:
options: Set the dial to about 200 C
Set the dial to about 160 C
Keep 180 C and bake for less time only
quiz.explain: The oven runs about 20 degrees hot, so she lowers the dial by 20 to reach a real 180 C.

quiz.q: Which reading best shows a lean white loaf is fully baked?
options: The top is pale but the loaf smells sweet
It has baked for exactly 20 minutes
quiz.explain: Lean bread is usually done at roughly 93 to 99 C in the centre. Time and colour alone can mislead.

modules.title: Professional Cakes: Sponges, Layers and Finishes
modules.overview: This module moves from one-tin cakes to the layered, finished cakes customers pay premium prices for. You will master the creaming method, the whisked genoise and the light chiffon, then learn to stack, fill, crumb-coat and finish a cake with buttercream or ganache that holds up in a warm climate.

lessons.title: The creaming method: a perfect Victoria sponge
objectives: Use the equal-weight Victoria sponge ratio to build a formula from your eggs
Cream butter and sugar correctly and add eggs without curdling
Fold in flour without knocking out air or developing gluten
Diagnose domed, sunken or dense sponges

blocks.text: The Victoria sponge is the classic test of a baker's creaming skill. Its formula is simple: **equal weights of egg, butter, caster sugar and self-raising flour**. Because the ratio is fixed, you can build the recipe from the eggs you actually have. Weigh your cracked eggs, then use the same weight of each of the other three ingredients.

blocks.name: shortcake
blocks.alt: A slice of layered sponge cake with cream and fruit
blocks.caption: A Victoria-style sponge is two light layers sandwiched with jam and cream or buttercream.

blocks.text: The base formula for two 20 cm tins

head: Ingredient
Weight
Note
rows: Soft enough to dent with a finger, not shiny
Fine sugar creams better than coarse granulated
Or 200 g plain flour plus about 8 to 10 g baking powder
Only to loosen to dropping consistency

blocks.title: The creaming method
items: Cream butter and sugar
Beat in eggs gradually
Fold in sifted flour
Loosen with milk
Bake at 180 C
blocks.caption: Each stage protects the air you trapped in the first step.

blocks.text: Creaming: the step most people rush

Beat the soft butter and caster sugar together for about 3 to 5 minutes with an electric mixer, longer by hand. You want the mixture to turn **pale, almost white, and fluffy**, with clearly more volume. This is not just mixing; you are cutting thousands of tiny air pockets into the butter. The baking powder later enlarges these pockets. Too little creaming gives a dense, heavy sponge no matter how fresh your powder is.

Beat the eggs lightly in a jug and add them a little at a time, beating well after each addition. Adding all the egg at once overloads the fat with water, and the mixture **curdles**: it looks grainy and split. If it starts to curdle, beat in one tablespoon of your measured flour. The flour soaks up the excess liquid and helps the emulsion recover.
Folding and baking

items: Sift the flour over the mixture in two additions.
Fold with a large metal spoon or spatula: cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom, and turn the batter over, rotating the bowl. Stop as soon as no dry flour shows.
Add milk only if needed, until the batter drops off the spoon in about 5 seconds.
Divide evenly between two greased and lined 20 cm tins. Weigh the tins to make sure the layers match.
Bake at 180 C (about 160 C fan) for roughly 20 to 25 minutes, until golden and springy and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool in the tins for 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack.

blocks.title: Worked example: building the formula from odd-sized eggs
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Owerri buys a crate of mixed eggs. For a three-tin version for a church event she cracks 7 eggs and they weigh 378 g.
steps: Equal weights: 378 g butter, 378 g caster sugar, 378 g self-raising flour.
Milk scales too: the base uses 30 ml for 200 g eggs, so 30 x 378 / 200 = about 57 ml. She adds it gradually and stops at 45 ml when the batter reaches dropping consistency.
Total batter is about 378 x 4 + 45 = 1,557 g. Divided between three 20 cm tins, each gets about 519 g.
She weighs each tin to 519 g, plus or minus 5 g, so all three layers bake in the same time.
blocks.result: Three even layers, all done at 23 minutes, with no wasted eggs and no guessing.

blocks.text: Reading your results

head: Fault
Likely cause
Fix next time
rows: Oven too hot, or too much flour
Check oven card; weigh flour accurately
Door opened too early, too much raising agent, or underbaked
Wait until at least two thirds of baking time; check leavener
Under-creamed, overmixed after flour, or butter too warm
Cream longer with cool soft butter; fold gently

blocks.text: Preparing tins properly

Grease the tin with soft butter or oil, line the base with a circle of baking paper, and grease the paper too. For straight sides on a cake you will stack, line the sides with a strip of paper that stands slightly above the rim. Fill tins no more than about two thirds full. If you only own one tin, keep the second portion of batter in a cool place and bake it straight after the first, but expect it to rise a little less, because double-acting baking powder has already started working.

Once you can make a reliable Victoria sponge, flavour variations are easy: replace 25 g of the flour with cocoa powder for chocolate, add the finely grated zest of two lemons or oranges for citrus, or dissolve two teaspoons of instant coffee in the milk for coffee. Keep the core ratio the same.

blocks.title: Hot kitchen creaming
blocks.text: If your kitchen is above about 28 C, cream in the early morning, keep butter in the fridge until 15 minutes before use, and stop to chill the bowl for 5 to 10 minutes if the mixture turns glossy.

takeaways: Victoria sponge equals equal weights of egg, butter, sugar and self-raising flour.
Cream until pale and fluffy: that air is your rise.
Add egg gradually; a spoon of flour rescues curdling.
Fold gently and weigh batter into tins for even layers.

activity.title: Bake a weighed Victoria sponge
steps: Weigh your shelled eggs and build the equal-weight formula from that number.
Cream for the full time and take a photo of the pale, fluffy mixture.
Weigh the batter into two tins and bake on your oven card setting.
Fill with jam and buttercream, cut one slice, and photograph the crumb.
activity.evidence: Your formula calculation, photo of the creamed mixture, and a photo of the cut slice.

lessons.title: Whisked sponges: genoise and chiffon
objectives: Whisk whole eggs and sugar to the ribbon stage for a genoise
Separate eggs and make a stable meringue for a chiffon cake
Fold flour and fat into a foam without losing volume
Choose between creamed, genoise and chiffon sponges for a given order

blocks.text: Creamed cakes get their air from butter. **Whisked sponges** get almost all their lift from eggs beaten into a foam. They are lighter and springier, they slice cleanly into thin layers, and they are the base of many gateaux and celebration cakes. Two classics matter most: the French **genoise**, made with whole eggs, and the **chiffon**, made with separated eggs and oil.

blocks.name: egg
blocks.caption: In whisked sponges the egg foam does the work that butter and baking powder do in creamed cakes.

blocks.text: Genoise: warm eggs to the ribbon

head: Ingredient (one 20 cm tin)
Weight
rows: Plain flour (or cake flour), sifted twice

items: Whisk eggs and sugar in a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, without the bowl touching the water, until just warm to the touch, about 40 to 45 C, and the sugar has dissolved.

Take it off the heat and whisk at high speed for about 8 to 10 minutes until the foam is pale, has roughly tripled in volume and reaches the **ribbon stage**: lifted whisk leaves a ribbon on the surface that holds for a few seconds.
Sift the flour over in three additions, folding gently each time.
Stir a large spoonful of batter into the warm melted butter, then fold that mixture back in. This stops the heavy butter sinking and deflating the foam.
Pour into a lined tin and bake at about 180 C for 20 to 25 minutes, until springy and shrinking slightly from the sides.

blocks.text: Warming the eggs helps the sugar dissolve and lets the proteins stretch further, so the foam is more stable. Genoise has little fat, so it is slightly dry on its own. That is intentional: professionals brush each layer with flavoured sugar syrup, which you will learn in the next lesson.
Chiffon: oil, yolks and meringue

A chiffon cake mixes an oil-and-yolk batter with a separate meringue. The oil keeps it moist and soft even after refrigeration, which is valuable in a hot climate where cream-filled cakes must be chilled. A typical 20 cm tube-tin chiffon uses about 5 eggs separated, 100 g cake flour, 100 g sugar split between the batter and the meringue, 60 ml oil, 75 ml water or milk, a teaspoon of baking powder, and a little cream of tartar or lemon juice to stabilise the whites.

items: Whisk yolks, part of the sugar, oil and liquid; sift in flour and baking powder and whisk smooth.

In a completely clean, grease-free bowl, whisk whites with cream of tartar until foamy, then add the remaining sugar gradually and whisk to **firm, glossy peaks** that stand up but are not dry or lumpy.
Stir one third of the meringue into the yolk batter to lighten it, then fold in the rest in two additions.
Pour into an **ungreased** tube tin. The batter needs to cling to the sides to climb.
Bake at about 160 to 170 C for 40 to 50 minutes. Turn upside down immediately and cool completely before releasing.

blocks.title: Why chiffon collapses
blocks.text: Grease in the whites (even a speck of yolk), over-whisked dry meringue, greasing the tin, or cooling the right way up all cause a chiffon to shrink and sink. Cooling upside down lets gravity hold the soft structure open until it firms.

blocks.title: Genoise or chiffon?
items: Genoise
Chiffon
blocks.caption: Choose genoise for stacked, structured cakes and chiffon for soft, cream-filled cakes kept in the fridge.

blocks.text: Both sponges freeze well. Wrap cooled layers tightly in cling film and then foil, freeze for up to about a month, and thaw in the fridge still wrapped so condensation forms on the wrapping, not the cake.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing the sponge for three orders
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Kano receives three orders in one week and must choose a sponge for each.
steps: Order 1: a fresh-cream and fruit cake that must be refrigerated. She chooses **chiffon**, because oil-based crumb stays soft at fridge temperature while butter sponges firm up.
Order 2: a three-layer cake with thin layers of mousse, cut clean for a photo. She chooses **genoise**, because it slices into even 1 cm layers and soaks up syrup without crumbling.
Order 3: a rich vanilla birthday cake covered in buttercream, eaten the same day at room temperature. She chooses the **creamed Victoria-style** sponge for its buttery flavour and sturdy crumb.
She notes bake temperatures: chiffon 165 C, genoise 180 C, creamed 180 C, and plans the chiffon first, since it must cool upside down for over an hour.
blocks.result: Each customer gets the sponge that suits the filling, storage and occasion, which is the difference between a home baker and a professional.

takeaways: Whisked sponges rise mainly on egg foam, not baking powder.
Genoise: warm eggs to about 40 to 45 C, whisk to the ribbon stage.
Chiffon: oil batter plus firm meringue, ungreased tin, cool upside down.
Match the sponge to the filling, storage and slicing needs.

activity.title: Ribbon and peak practice
steps: Make one genoise and photograph the ribbon stage before adding flour.
Make one chiffon and photograph the firm, glossy meringue.
Cut both cakes after cooling and compare height, softness and moisture.
Write which orders you would use each one for.
activity.evidence: Photos of the ribbon stage, the meringue peaks and both cut cakes, with your comparison notes.

lessons.title: Building a layer cake: levelling, syrup, filling and crumb coat
objectives: Level and split cakes into even layers
Make and apply a soaking syrup in the right amount
Build a buttercream dam so soft fillings do not leak
Apply and set a crumb coat ready for a clean final finish

blocks.text: A professional layer cake looks straight, tall and neat from every side, and every slice shows even stripes of cake and filling. That comes from a fixed sequence of steps, each one done before the next. Most problems customers notice, like a leaning cake, crumbs in the icing or filling oozing out, come from skipping one of these steps.

blocks.name: birthday-cake
blocks.caption: Neat layers and a clean finish start with levelling, syrup, a dam and a crumb coat.

blocks.title: Layer cake assembly order
items: Cool and chill layers
Level and split
Soak with syrup
Dam and fill
Crumb coat and chill
blocks.caption: Chilling between stages is what keeps everything straight and crumb free.

blocks.text: Your basic assembly tools

items: **Cake board:** a thin card circle the same size as the cake, so the cake can be moved and later stacked.
**Cake drum:** a thicker board 5 to 8 cm wider than the cake, for display and delivery.
**Turntable:** lets you spin the cake while scraping; a heavy plate on an upturned bowl is a workable start.
**Bench scraper and offset spatula:** the scraper makes straight sides; the spatula spreads icing and smooths tops.
**Piping bag and round nozzle:** for the buttercream dam, even without decorating skills.

blocks.text: Cool, wrap, chill

Never assemble a warm cake: buttercream melts and layers slide. Cool layers completely on a rack, wrap them in cling film, and chill for at least an hour or overnight. A cold cake has a firmer crumb, makes fewer crumbs when cut and is much easier to stack.
Levelling and splitting

items: Place the cake on a turntable or an upturned plate on a non-slip mat.
With a long serrated knife held level, cut off the dome using a gentle sawing motion while turning the cake.
To split a layer, mark the halfway height with toothpicks every few centimetres around the side, then cut along the line.
Keep the flat bottom crust of the lowest layer facing down onto the board, and put the last layer cut side down on top, so the top surface is the smooth base of a layer.

blocks.text: Soaking syrup

A simple syrup is equal weights of sugar and water, boiled just until the sugar dissolves, then cooled. You can flavour it with vanilla, citrus zest or coffee. Brush it evenly over each layer with a pastry brush. Genoise needs it; creamed cakes benefit from a lighter touch. Too much syrup makes a soggy, sweet cake that can collapse under its own weight.
Dam, fill, stack

Pipe a ring of stiff buttercream about 1 cm thick around the top edge of each layer. This **dam** holds soft fillings like jam, curd, fresh cream or fruit inside the cake. Spread the filling inside the ring to the same height as the dam, add the next layer, press down gently and check it is level from the side.
The crumb coat

Spread a thin layer of buttercream or ganache over the whole cake, top and sides, and scrape it smooth with a bench scraper. It should be thin enough that you can see the cake through it in places. This seals loose crumbs into a layer that will never be seen. Chill the cake for 20 to 30 minutes until the coat is firm to the touch, then apply the final, thicker coat with clean icing.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a three-layer 20 cm cake
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Abuja is assembling a 20 cm vanilla cake with three genoise layers, strawberry jam and Swiss meringue buttercream for a Saturday party.
steps: Syrup: she boils 100 g sugar with 100 g water, which gives about 150 ml of syrup once dissolved.
Each layer gets about 3 tablespoons (45 ml) brushed evenly: 3 x 45 = 135 ml, leaving a little spare.
Two filling levels: a buttercream dam on each, then about 100 g jam spread inside each dam (200 g in total).
Crumb coat Friday evening, chill 30 minutes, final coat, then refrigerate overnight in a clean, covered cake box.
Saturday: she takes it out about 1 hour before serving so the buttercream softens, and keeps it out of direct sun.
blocks.result: A level, neat cake with no crumbs in the finish and no jam leaking, made without a last-minute rush.

blocks.title: Fillings and food safety
blocks.text: Fresh cream, custards, curds, cream cheese icings and fresh fruit fillings are perishable. Keep cakes with these fillings refrigerated, tell the customer to keep them cold, and follow the general food safety rule of not leaving perishable food at room temperature for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is very hot (above about 32 C). Wash hands, tools and boards, and keep raw eggs away from finished cakes.

takeaways: Assemble only cold, fully cooled layers.
Level and split with a serrated knife and toothpick guides.
Syrup moistens; a buttercream dam holds soft fillings in.
A thin, chilled crumb coat makes the final finish clean.

activity.title: Assemble and crumb-coat one cake
steps: Bake two layers and chill them overnight.
Level and split them into four thin layers.
Make syrup, brush each layer, and fill using a buttercream dam.
Apply a crumb coat, chill it, and photograph the cake from the side to check it is straight.
activity.evidence: Side and top photos of your crumb-coated cake, plus one photo of a cut slice showing the layers.

lessons.title: Buttercreams and ganache that survive the heat
objectives: Make American and Swiss meringue buttercream and know when to use each
Heat egg whites to a safe temperature for meringue buttercream
Use ganache ratios for drips, fillings and firm coatings
Plan finishes that hold up in warm, humid weather

blocks.text: The finish is the first thing a customer sees and the part most affected by Nigerian heat. Butter starts to soften at around room temperature and melts not far above it, so a buttercream that is perfect in an air-conditioned room may slide in a hall at 32 C. Knowing several finishes and their ratios lets you choose one that suits the venue, not just the picture the customer sent.

blocks.name: chocolate-bar
blocks.caption: Chocolate and cream make ganache, which sets firmer and handles heat better than most buttercreams.

blocks.text: American buttercream

Beat softened butter until pale, then beat in sifted icing sugar at about **1 part butter to 2 parts icing sugar** by weight, with a pinch of salt, vanilla and a spoon or two of milk to adjust. It is quick, sweet and crusts slightly on the surface. Replacing part of the butter with a good vegetable shortening raises its heat tolerance, though it changes the taste and mouthfeel.
Swiss meringue buttercream (SMBC)
SMBC is silky, less sweet and pipes beautifully. A common ratio is about **1 part egg white, 2 parts sugar and 3 parts butter** by weight, for example 100 g whites, 200 g sugar and 300 g butter.

items: Whisk whites and sugar in a clean heatproof bowl over simmering water until the sugar dissolves and the mixture reaches **71 C** on a probe thermometer. This is the safe temperature for egg dishes and reduces the risk from bacteria such as Salmonella.
Whisk at high speed until the meringue is thick, glossy and the bowl feels cool, about 10 minutes.
Add soft butter a piece at a time. It may look curdled or soupy midway: keep whisking. Soupy means too warm (chill the bowl 10 minutes); curdled means too cold (warm the bowl sides briefly).
Finish with vanilla and a pinch of salt. Store covered in the fridge and re-whip before use.

blocks.text: Ganache: two ingredients, many jobs

Ganache is chocolate melted into hot cream. Bring cream just to a simmer, pour over chopped chocolate, wait 2 minutes, then stir from the centre outward until glossy. The ratio of chocolate to cream decides how firm it sets.

head: Use
Dark chocolate : cream
White chocolate : cream
Set
rows: Firm coating under fondant, sharp edges

blocks.text: White and milk chocolate have more milk solids and cocoa butter and less cocoa solids, so they need much more chocolate to set firm. Compound or cooking chocolate, which replaces cocoa butter with other fats, sets differently: test a small batch before a big order.

blocks.title: Choosing a finish
items: SMBC or whipped ganache
Firm ganache
American buttercream
Ganache under fondant
axes: Heat at the venue (low to high)
blocks.caption: The hotter the venue and the sharper the finish required, the more you move towards firm ganache.

blocks.title: Worked example: ganache for a drip cake
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Lagos is finishing a 15 cm tall, 20 cm wide cake covered in firm dark ganache with a contrasting drip, for an outdoor event in the afternoon.
steps: Coating: she uses the 2 : 1 ratio, 600 g dark chocolate and 300 g cream, enough for a crumb coat and final coat with a little spare.
Drip: she uses 1 : 1, 100 g dark chocolate and 100 g cream, and cools it to just warm, about 30 to 32 C, so it runs partway down without pooling.
She tests one drip on the side of the chilled cake before doing the whole edge.
She chills the finished cake until firm, delivers it in a cool vehicle, and asks the venue to keep it shaded and indoors until serving.
blocks.result: The firm 2 : 1 ganache keeps sharp edges much longer in the heat than a butter-based finish, and the drip stops neatly halfway down.

blocks.text: Colouring and flavouring finishes

Use gel food colours rather than liquid ones: they are concentrated, so they do not thin the icing. Colours deepen as they rest, so mix a shade slightly lighter than the target and leave it covered for an hour before judging. Very dark shades like black or deep red are easier to reach in chocolate buttercream or by starting from a cocoa base. Flavour SMBC by beating in cooled melted chocolate, fruit purees reduced until thick, or finely ground nuts, a little at a time, tasting as you go.

blocks.title: Weather plan
blocks.text: For outdoor or un-air-conditioned venues, steer customers towards ganache, a crusting buttercream or fondant over ganache, and avoid whipped cream finishes. Explain the reason in your quote: it shows expertise and protects your reputation.

takeaways: American buttercream is about 1 butter to 2 icing sugar.
SMBC: heat whites and sugar to 71 C before whipping.
Ganache firmness depends on the chocolate to cream ratio.
Choose finishes for the venue's heat, not only the photo.

activity.title: Heat test three finishes
steps: Make small batches of American buttercream, SMBC and 2 : 1 dark ganache.
Spread each on a separate small cake or upturned plate.
Leave them side by side at room temperature for 2 hours, out of direct sun.
Photograph them at the start and after 2 hours and record which held its shape best.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos with a short note naming your best finish for a hot venue.

quiz.q: Nneka's shelled eggs weigh 260 g. Using the Victoria sponge ratio, how much butter does she need?
quiz.explain: A Victoria sponge uses equal weights of egg, butter, sugar and self-raising flour, so 260 g butter.

quiz.q: Her creamed mixture splits and looks grainy while she adds the eggs. What should she do next?
options: Beat in a tablespoon of the measured flour and add the remaining egg more slowly
Put it straight in the oven
quiz.explain: Flour absorbs the excess liquid and helps the emulsion recover; adding egg gradually prevents it splitting again.

quiz.q: Which sponge is the best choice for a fresh-cream cake that must stay in the fridge until served?
options: Chiffon, because its oil-based crumb stays soft when cold
Any butter sponge, because butter stays soft in the fridge
quiz.explain: Oil stays liquid at fridge temperature, so chiffon stays soft; butter sponges firm up when chilled.

quiz.q: A chiffon cake shrinks badly after baking. Which mistake is a likely cause?
options: Adding cream of tartar to the whites
quiz.explain: Chiffon batter must cling to an ungreased tin to climb and hold its height while cooling upside down.

quiz.q: Why do bakers pipe a ring of stiff buttercream before adding jam or cream between layers?
options: To act as a dam that keeps soft filling inside the cake
To make the cake taller only
quiz.explain: The dam holds soft fillings in so they do not leak out or push layers sideways.

quiz.q: To what temperature should egg whites and sugar be heated for Swiss meringue buttercream?
quiz.explain: 71 C (160 F) is the recognised safe temperature for egg dishes; it also dissolves the sugar.

quiz.q: Which ganache ratio gives a firm dark chocolate coating suitable for sharp edges or under fondant?
quiz.explain: More chocolate gives a firmer set. 2 : 1 dark ganache is firm at room temperature.

modules.title: Pastry: Shortcrust, Rough Puff and Choux
modules.overview: Pastry rewards precise temperature control more than any other branch of baking. This module teaches the three pastries every professional must master: tender shortcrust for tarts and pies, flaky rough puff, and steam-raised choux. It ends with a systematic way to diagnose and fix pastry faults.

lessons.title: Shortcrust and sweet pastry: tarts with crisp bases
objectives: Make savoury shortcrust at the classic 2 : 1 flour to fat ratio
Make a sweet pastry (pate sucree) for dessert tarts
Rest, roll and line a tart tin without shrinkage
Blind bake a case so the base is crisp, not soggy

blocks.text: Shortcrust is called short because the fat shortens the gluten, so the pastry snaps and crumbles instead of stretching. The classic ratio is **2 parts flour to 1 part fat** by weight, plus a pinch of salt and just enough cold water to bind. You already know it from Nigerian meat pie. In this lesson you will push it further into professional open tarts, which need thinner, crisper, perfectly shaped cases.

blocks.name: pie
blocks.alt: A baked pie with a golden crust
blocks.caption: A crisp, golden shortcrust comes from cold fat, little water and a fully baked base.

blocks.text: Two doughs to master

head: Savoury shortcrust
Sweet pastry (pate sucree)
rows: 100 g cold butter (or half butter, half baking fat)
80 to 100 g icing sugar, pinch of salt
Rub fat into flour, then add water
Cream butter and sugar, add egg, then flour
Fruit tarts, custard tarts, lemon tarts

blocks.text: Method for savoury shortcrust

items: Cut cold butter into 1 cm cubes and toss them in the flour and salt.
Rub in with your fingertips (or pulse in a food processor) until the mixture looks like fine breadcrumbs with a few pea-sized pieces of fat left. Work quickly so the butter stays cold.
Sprinkle in most of the water and mix with a table knife. Squeeze a handful: if it holds together, stop. Add the last water only if it still crumbles.
Press into a flat disc, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes. This relaxes the gluten and firms the fat.

blocks.text: Rolling and lining without shrinkage

Roll the chilled dough on a lightly floured surface to about 3 mm thick, turning it a quarter turn after every few rolls so it stays round and does not stick. Lift it over the rolling pin, lay it into the tin and **ease it down into the corners** rather than stretching it. Stretched pastry pulls back in the oven. Leave a little overhang, then chill the lined tin for another 20 to 30 minutes before baking.

blocks.title: Blind baking a tart case
items: Line, prick and chill
Paper and baking beans
Bake about 15 minutes
Remove beans, bake 5 to 10 minutes
Brush egg, bake 2 minutes
blocks.caption: Baking the case before filling sets and dries the base so it stays crisp under wet fillings.

blocks.text: **Blind baking** means baking the empty case first. Line it with crumpled baking paper and fill with ceramic baking beans, dried beans or uncooked rice, which stop the base puffing and the sides sliding. Bake at about 190 to 200 C for roughly 15 minutes, lift out the paper and beans, then bake another 5 to 10 minutes until the base is dry and lightly golden. For very wet fillings like custard, brush the hot case with beaten egg and return it for 2 minutes. The egg seals any tiny holes.

blocks.title: Worked example: tart cases for an order of 40 mini tarts
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Asaba is making 40 mini lemon tarts, 7 cm across, using sweet pastry. She tested one case and it needed 18 g of dough.
steps: Dough needed: 40 x 18 g = 720 g. She adds about 10% for trimmings: 720 x 1.1 = 792 g.
Her base sweet pastry batch weighs 250 + 125 + 90 + 50 = 515 g (using 90 g icing sugar).
Batches needed: 792 / 515 = about 1.54, so she makes 1.5 batches: 375 g flour, 188 g butter, 135 g icing sugar and 75 g egg (about one and a half eggs, beaten and weighed).
1.5 batches weigh about 773 g. That covers 40 cases at 18 g (720 g) with 53 g for re-rolling.
She blind bakes trays of 12 at 190 C, sealing each case with egg because the lemon filling is wet.
blocks.result: Forty even, crisp cases with very little waste, and a recorded yield (18 g per 7 cm case) she can reuse for every future quote.

blocks.text: Storing and freezing pastry

Wrapped shortcrust keeps in the fridge for about 2 days and freezes well for about a month; thaw it in the fridge overnight. You can also freeze lined, unbaked tart cases and blind bake them straight from frozen, adding a few minutes. Baked empty cases stay crisp for a few days in an airtight tin, which lets you spread a big order over several days and only fill on the day of delivery.

blocks.title: Cold hands, cold room
blocks.text: Rinse your hands in cold water and dry them before rubbing in. If the dough becomes soft and sticky while rolling, slide it onto a tray and chill it for 10 minutes rather than adding more flour, which toughens the pastry.

takeaways: Savoury shortcrust: 2 parts flour to 1 part cold fat, minimal water.
Sweet pastry uses icing sugar and egg for a crisp, biscuit-like case.
Ease pastry into the tin; stretching causes shrinkage.
Blind bake and seal with egg for crisp bases under wet fillings.

activity.title: Blind bake six tart cases
steps: Make one batch of sweet pastry and chill it.
Weigh the dough you use for one case and record it.
Line, chill and blind bake six cases, sealing three of them with egg.
Fill all six with the same wet filling and compare the bases after 2 hours.
activity.evidence: Photos of the empty cases and a cut tart from each group, with your dough-per-case weight noted.

lessons.title: Rough puff pastry: lamination made practical
objectives: Explain how layers of fat and steam create flaky pastry
Make rough puff pastry using letter folds
Calculate how folding multiplies layers
Plan chilling and timing to laminate successfully in a hot climate

blocks.text: Flaky pastry works by **lamination**: building many thin, separate layers of dough and fat. In the oven, the water in the dough and butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the fat stops them from sticking back together. Full puff pastry wraps one big block of butter in dough. **Rough puff** is faster: cubes of butter are mixed loosely into the dough and then flattened into streaks by rolling and folding. It rises a little less evenly but is excellent for sausage rolls, turnovers, palmiers and pie lids.

blocks.name: croissant
blocks.caption: Croissants and rough puff both rise because steam separates layers of dough and fat.

blocks.text: Formula

head: Ingredient
Weight
Percentage of flour
rows: Cold butter, cut into 2 cm cubes
Small amount, helps the dough stay supple

blocks.text: Method

items: Toss the butter cubes in the flour and salt. Do not rub them in: you want whole lumps.
Add most of the water and mix into a rough, shaggy dough with visible butter pieces. Add more water only if dry flour remains.
Shape into a rectangle, wrap and chill 20 minutes.
Roll into a long rectangle about three times as long as it is wide, keeping the edges straight.
**Letter fold:** fold the bottom third up, then the top third down over it, like folding a letter. Turn the dough a quarter turn so the open edge faces you.
Roll and fold again. That is two folds. Wrap, chill 20 to 30 minutes, then do two more folds. Chill again before shaping.

blocks.title: The lamination cycle
items: Roll into a long rectangle
Letter fold in three
Quarter turn
Chill when soft
Repeat to four folds
blocks.caption: Each cycle multiplies layers; chilling stops the butter melting into the dough.

blocks.text: Why the number of folds matters

Each letter fold stacks the dough in three, so it roughly triples the number of layers. After 1 fold you have about 3 layers, after 2 folds 9, after 3 folds 27, and after 4 folds 81. Classic puff pastry is often given six folds, which in theory gives 729 layers. More folds are not always better: if the layers get too thin, the butter breaks through and the pastry rises less. For rough puff, four folds is the usual target.

blocks.title: The heat problem
blocks.text: Lamination fails when the butter melts into the dough. Then you get a tough, greasy bread-like pastry, not flakes. Work early in the morning or in an air-conditioned space, chill the dough whenever butter starts to look soft or shiny, flour the surface lightly, and brush off excess flour before each fold.
Shaping and baking

Use a very sharp knife or cutter and cut straight down. A blunt knife presses the layers together at the edges and they cannot rise. Do not let egg wash drip over the cut edges for the same reason. Chill shaped pieces for 15 to 20 minutes, then bake in a fully preheated oven at about 200 to 220 C, so steam forms fast. Bake until deep golden; pale puff pastry is often raw and doughy inside.

blocks.title: Worked example: a laminating schedule for 48 sausage rolls
blocks.context: For example, Aisha in Abuja has an order for 48 cocktail sausage rolls for Saturday 4 pm. Her kitchen reaches about 30 C by midday. One batch of rough puff (about 630 g) makes about 24 small rolls.
steps: Batches: 48 / 24 = 2 batches, about 1,260 g of pastry.
Friday 6 am: mix both doughs, chill 20 minutes, give each two folds, chill. 7 am: two more folds each, wrap and refrigerate overnight.
Friday evening: make and chill the sausage filling separately in a covered container.
Saturday 7 am: roll, fill, cut and chill the rolls on lined trays for 20 minutes.
Bake at 210 C for about 20 to 25 minutes until deep golden and the filling is cooked through; cool and pack by 11 am, then keep covered and deliver within the safe holding time.
blocks.result: By doing all the lamination before the kitchen heats up and resting overnight, Aisha gets crisp, flaky rolls and finishes hours ahead of the deadline.

blocks.text: Rough puff also freezes very well. Wrap the finished, folded block tightly and freeze it, or freeze shaped, unbaked pieces on a tray and then bag them. Bake from frozen at the same temperature for a few minutes longer. This is how many small bakeries keep stock ready for last-minute orders.

blocks.title: Meat fillings
blocks.text: Cook sausage or minced meat fillings thoroughly and check the centre of one roll is piping hot and no longer pink. Keep raw meat, its boards and knives completely separate from the pastry and finished products.

takeaways: Steam plus separate fat layers create flakes.
Rough puff uses whole butter cubes rolled into streaks with letter folds.
Each letter fold roughly triples the layers: four folds gives about 81.
Keep butter cold, cut cleanly, and bake hot.

activity.title: Laminate and compare
steps: Make one batch of rough puff, giving four letter folds with chilling.
Cut six squares with a sharp knife and six with a blunt one.
Bake all twelve on one tray at 210 C.
Compare the height and layering of both sets.
activity.evidence: A photo of both sets side by side and one cut in half to show the layers, with notes on what you saw.

lessons.title: Choux pastry and creme patissiere
objectives: Cook a choux panade and add eggs to the correct consistency
Pipe and bake choux so shells are hollow, crisp and do not collapse
Make a safe, smooth creme patissiere filling
Calculate shell and filling yields for an order

blocks.text: Choux pastry is unusual: it is cooked twice. First you cook flour in boiling water and butter on the stove to make a thick paste called a **panade**. Then you beat in eggs and bake it. There is no yeast or baking powder. The paste is full of water, which turns to steam in a hot oven and blows each piece up like a balloon, while the egg proteins and starch set around the steam into a hollow, crisp shell. Profiteroles, eclairs, choux buns and croquembouche all come from this one paste.

blocks.name: chef
blocks.caption: Choux depends on precise technique at the stove, then a hot, undisturbed oven.

blocks.text: Formula

head: Ingredient
Weight
rows: About 220 to 250 g (4 to 5 large), added gradually

items: Heat water, milk, butter, salt and sugar until the butter melts and the liquid comes to a full rolling boil.
Take the pan off the heat, tip in all the flour at once and beat hard with a wooden spoon until smooth.
Return to medium heat and keep stirring for 1 to 2 minutes, until the paste comes away from the sides and a thin film forms on the bottom of the pan. This dries the paste so it can absorb more egg.
Transfer to a bowl and beat for a minute or two to release steam, until just warm.
Add the egg a little at a time, beating fully after each addition.

blocks.text: The V test: knowing when to stop adding egg

Eggs vary in size and flours absorb differently, so you never add a fixed amount. Lift the spoon or spatula out of the paste. When it is ready, the paste falls slowly and leaves a **V-shaped flag** hanging from the edge, and a finger drawn through the paste leaves a trench that slowly closes. Too stiff, and the shells crack and stay small. Too runny, and they spread flat. If you add too much egg, you cannot take it out: that is why you add the last portion slowly.

blocks.title: Choux success checks
items: Film on pan bottom
Paste just warm before eggs
V-shaped flag on spatula
Hot oven, door closed
Deep golden, dry shells
blocks.caption: Miss any one of these checks and the shells are likely to be flat, soggy or collapsed.

blocks.text: Piping and baking

Pipe with a 1 cm round or open star nozzle onto a lined tray, holding the bag upright. For profiteroles, pipe rounds about 4 cm across; for eclairs, lines about 10 to 12 cm long. Flatten any peaks with a wet fingertip. Bake at about 200 C for 15 minutes, then reduce to about 180 C for another 15 to 20 minutes **without opening the door**. When they are deep golden and feel light and dry, pierce each underneath with a skewer to release steam and return them to the switched-off oven, door ajar, for 5 to 10 minutes to dry.
Creme patissiere (pastry cream)

Heat 500 ml milk with vanilla. In a bowl whisk 4 egg yolks (about 80 g), 100 g sugar and 40 g cornflour until pale. Pour the hot milk onto the yolks while whisking, return everything to the pan, and whisk over medium heat until it thickens and then **bubbles for a full 1 to 2 minutes**. Boiling is needed to cook the starch and to make the egg safe. Off the heat, whisk in 30 g butter. Pour into a clean shallow dish, press cling film onto the surface to stop a skin forming, cool quickly and refrigerate.

blocks.title: Pastry cream is high risk
blocks.text: Egg and milk custards are an ideal place for bacteria to grow. Cool pastry cream quickly in a shallow container, keep it refrigerated, use it within about 2 days, fill shells as close to serving as possible, and keep filled pastries chilled. Never leave filled choux in a warm room or a hot car for hours.

blocks.title: Worked example: profiteroles for 40 guests
blocks.context: For example, Uche in Enugu is quoting for a dessert table: 40 guests, 2 cream-filled profiteroles each.
steps: Shells needed: 40 x 2 = 80, plus 10% spare for cracked or uneven ones: 88 shells.
Her test shows one 4 cm shell uses about 15 g of paste. 88 x 15 g = 1,320 g of paste.

One batch above (water, milk, butter, flour, about 235 g egg) gives roughly 650 g of paste after cooking, so she needs 1,320 / 650 = about 2 batches. She makes them one after the other, not as one double batch, so the paste cooks evenly.
Filling: about 18 g of pastry cream per shell, 80 x 18 = 1,440 g. One pastry cream batch makes about 720 g, so she makes 2 batches.
She bakes shells the day before and keeps them in an airtight tin, makes the cream the day before and chills it, then fills on the morning of the event and keeps them refrigerated until delivery.
blocks.result: Uche orders exactly the eggs, milk and butter she needs and serves crisp shells with safe, cold filling.

takeaways: Choux is cooked on the stove, then baked; steam is its only leavener.
Dry the panade until a film forms, then add egg until the V test passes.
Bake hot without opening the door, then pierce and dry the shells.
Boil pastry cream for 1 to 2 minutes, chill fast and keep filled choux cold.

activity.title: Profiterole practice batch
steps: Make one batch of choux and photograph the V test.
Pipe 20 profiteroles, weighing the paste for one of them.
Bake, pierce and dry the shells; cut one open to check it is hollow.
Make pastry cream, chill it and fill half the shells; record how much cream each took.
activity.evidence: Photos of the V test, a cut shell and filled profiteroles, plus your paste and filling weights per piece.

lessons.title: Diagnosing and fixing pastry faults
objectives: Use a step by step method to trace a pastry fault back to its cause
Identify the causes of shrinkage, toughness, sogginess and poor rise
Keep a batch record that makes faults easier to diagnose
Decide whether a faulty batch can be rescued or must be discarded

blocks.text: Every pastry fault has a cause you can find. Professionals do not say the pastry just did not work. They ask which of four things went wrong: **ingredients and ratio, temperature, handling, or baking**. Working through these in order turns a disappointing batch into a lesson you only need to learn once.

blocks.name: cooking
blocks.alt: A person cooking in a kitchen
blocks.caption: Careful records at each stage make pastry faults easy to trace.

blocks.title: Fault diagnosis order
items: Describe the fault exactly
Check ratio and weighing
Check dough and room temperature
Check handling and resting
Check oven and bake time
blocks.caption: Work from left to right; the first cause you find is usually the main one.

blocks.text: Shortcrust faults

head: Fault
Likely causes
Fix
rows: Pastry stretched into tin; not rested; too much water
Ease in, chill 30 minutes before baking, use less water
Overworked, too much water or flour on the board
Rub in lightly, add water gradually, chill instead of adding flour
Too little water or butter rubbed in too finely
Add water a teaspoon at a time; leave some pea-sized fat
Not blind baked, wet filling, oven too cool, tin on a cold shelf
Blind bake fully, seal with egg, bake on a preheated tray

blocks.text: Rough puff faults

head: Fault
Likely causes
Fix
rows: Butter melted into dough during folding
Chill between folds, work in cool hours
Butter leaks out and fries in the tray
Oven too cool, so fat melts before steam lifts the layers
Uneven rolling, folds not squared, blunt cutter
Bake to deep golden; roll thinner

blocks.text: Choux faults

head: Fault
Likely causes
Fix
rows: Too much egg, paste too runny
Add the last egg slowly, use the V test
Too little egg, paste too stiff
Add egg until the V test passes
Bake until deep golden and dry; keep door closed
Not dried, filled too early, humid storage
Pierce and dry; store airtight; fill close to serving

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a soggy custard tart
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin sells egg custard tarts. A café returns a tray because the bases are soft and pale.
steps: Describe exactly: bases pale and wet underneath, sides fine, filling set.
Ratio: her batch record shows the usual 200 g flour, 100 g butter, 45 ml water. No change.
Temperature and handling: the dough was rested and chilled as usual.
Baking: her record shows she skipped the egg seal because she was rushing, and baked the filled tarts on the bottom shelf, which her oven card says runs cooler.
Fix: blind bake to light golden, seal with egg, and bake filled tarts on the middle shelf on a preheated metal tray.
blocks.result: The next batch has crisp golden bases. Her batch record found the real cause in minutes instead of her changing the recipe at random.

blocks.text: Keep a batch record

For every production batch, note the date, product, ingredient weights, room temperature, chilling times, oven setting, shelf, bake time and result. A notebook or a simple WhatsApp note to yourself is enough. When something goes wrong, you compare it with a good batch and the difference usually jumps out.
Common faults in all pastry

items: **Pale colour:** oven too cool, no egg wash, or too little sugar in sweet pastry. Bake longer or hotter and egg wash evenly.
**Burnt base, raw top:** heat coming mainly from below. Move up a shelf or slide an empty tray underneath as a shield.
**Bubbled, puffed base in a tart:** the case was not pricked or weighted. Prick with a fork and use baking beans.
**Pastry tastes floury or bland:** too much dusting flour or no salt. Brush off excess flour and always include a pinch of salt.
**Uneven bake across the tray:** oven hot spots. Turn the tray once the pastry has set and check your oven card.

blocks.text: Change only one thing at a time when you test a fix. If you change the water, the oven shelf and the resting time all at once and the pastry improves, you will not know which change worked, and the fault may come back.

blocks.title: When to throw it away
blocks.text: Shape faults can sometimes be rescued: broken shells become a trifle, misshapen puff becomes palmiers for your family. But anything with a food safety doubt, such as filled pastries left warm for hours or a filling that smells or tastes off, must be discarded, never sold.

takeaways: Check ratio, temperature, handling, then baking, in that order.
Shrinkage comes from stretching and too little rest.
Greasy flat puff means the butter melted too early.
A batch record turns faults into fast fixes.

activity.title: Start your batch record
steps: Create a batch record template with the fields listed in this lesson.
Fill it in for your next three pastry batches.
Deliberately make one small fault test (for example, stretch one tart case into its tin) and record the result.
Write the cause and fix for any fault you saw.
activity.evidence: Photos of three completed batch records and your fault test result.

quiz.q: Tolu has 300 g flour for a savoury shortcrust. Using the classic ratio, how much fat does she need?
quiz.explain: Shortcrust is 2 parts flour to 1 part fat, so 300 g flour needs 150 g fat.

quiz.q: Her tart cases shrank down the sides of the tins. What is the most likely cause?
options: She chilled the lined tins before baking
She stretched the pastry into the tins and did not rest it
quiz.explain: Stretched, unrested gluten pulls back in the heat. Ease pastry in and chill before baking.

quiz.q: After four letter folds, roughly how many layers does rough puff have?
quiz.explain: Each letter fold triples the layers: 3, 9, 27, 81.

quiz.q: Rough puff comes out flat, greasy and bread-like. What most likely happened?
options: The butter melted into the dough during folding
quiz.explain: When butter melts into the dough the layers are lost, so steam cannot separate them.

quiz.q: During choux making, how does Ada know she has added enough egg?
options: The paste falls slowly from the spatula leaving a V-shaped flag
The paste is stiff enough to roll into balls
quiz.explain: The V test shows the right consistency regardless of egg size or flour.

quiz.q: Why must creme patissiere bubble for 1 to 2 minutes?
options: To cook the starch so it sets smoothly and to make the egg safe
quiz.explain: Boiling cooks the cornflour fully and heats the egg to a safe temperature.

quiz.q: Custard tart bases come back soft and pale. What should be checked first in her batch record?
options: The colour of the tart tins only
Whether the case was blind baked, sealed and baked on the right shelf
quiz.explain: Soggy bases usually come from incomplete blind baking, no egg seal, or a cool baking position.

modules.title: Artisan and Enriched Bread
modules.overview: Good bread is mostly about controlling time and temperature. This module teaches how to manage yeast and fermentation in a hot climate, how to divide, shape, proof and score loaves with confidence, and how to make rich, soft enriched breads such as brioche and a tangzhong milk bread.

lessons.title: Yeast, fermentation and dough temperature
objectives: Convert between instant, active dry and fresh yeast
Calculate the water temperature needed to hit a target dough temperature
Use a preferment or the fridge to build flavour and control timing
Judge when bulk fermentation is finished

blocks.text: Baker's yeast is a living single-celled fungus. In dough it feeds on sugars released from flour starch and produces **carbon dioxide**, which inflates the gluten, and **alcohol and acids**, which give bread its flavour. Yeast is very sensitive to temperature. It is slow in the cold, works steadily around 24 to 27 C, races in the heat, and is killed at around 60 C. In a Nigerian kitchen that is often above 30 C, the real skill is slowing yeast down, not speeding it up.

blocks.name: bread
blocks.caption: Every loaf is a record of how well the yeast was managed during fermentation.

blocks.text: Types of yeast and conversions

head: Type
How to use
Relative amount
rows: Dissolve in some of the warm liquid for 5 to 10 minutes first
Crumble into the liquid; keep refrigerated, short life
About 2.5 to 3 times the instant amount

blocks.text: Salt at around 2% of flour weight strengthens gluten and controls yeast, but concentrated salt directly on yeast slows it, so mix salt into the flour rather than onto the yeast. Sugar up to about 5% helps yeast; above about 10% it starts to slow it, which is why rich doughs need more yeast or more time.
Desired dough temperature

Professional bakers aim for a set **desired dough temperature (DDT)**, often 24 to 26 C, at the end of mixing. Then fermentation times become predictable. The only temperature you can easily control is the water, so you calculate it with this simple rule for a straight dough:

items: Multiply your target dough temperature by 3.
Subtract the room temperature, the flour temperature and the friction factor (the heat added by mixing: roughly a few degrees by hand, more in a machine; measure it once for your mixer).
The answer is the water temperature you need.

blocks.title: Worked example: cool water for a hot kitchen
blocks.context: For example, Efe in Warri wants her dough at 25 C. Her room is 31 C, her flour is 30 C, and her stand mixer adds about 6 C of friction.
steps: Target x 3: 25 x 3 = 75.
Subtract room, flour and friction: 75 - 31 - 30 - 6 = 8.
She needs water at about 8 C, so she uses water from the fridge and checks it with a thermometer.
She measures the dough after mixing: 25.5 C. Close enough.
With a warm dough of 30 C her bulk rise used to finish in about 45 minutes and the bread tasted flat. At 25 C it takes about 90 minutes and the flavour is clearly better.
blocks.result: By controlling water temperature Efe gets consistent timing and better flavour, and she writes her friction factor on her oven card for future batches.

blocks.title: Stages of a yeasted dough
items: Mix and develop gluten
Bulk fermentation
Divide and pre-shape
Final shape and proof
Score and bake
blocks.caption: Temperature control during bulk fermentation decides most of the flavour and texture.

blocks.text: Developing gluten: the windowpane test

Knead or machine-mix until the dough is smooth and elastic. Then pinch off a small piece and stretch it gently between your fingers. If it stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing, the gluten is well developed. If it tears quickly, mix a few minutes more. Enriched doughs need especially strong development before the butter goes in.
Preferments and cold fermentation

A **preferment** is part of the flour, water and a tiny amount of yeast mixed hours ahead. A **poolish**, for example, is equal weights of flour and water with roughly 0.1% instant yeast, left about 12 to 16 hours at cool room temperature until bubbly and domed. It gives more flavour, better keeping and a more open crumb. You can also **retard** a dough by putting it in the fridge for 8 to 16 hours. Cold slows the yeast but lets flavour develop, and it lets you shape at night and bake fresh at dawn.
When is bulk fermentation done?

items: The dough has grown clearly, often by around 50 to 100% depending on the formula (use a straight-sided container with a mark).
The surface is domed and smooth with some bubbles at the sides.
It feels airy, wobbly and less sticky when you move the container.
Time is only a guide: the same dough can take twice as long on a cool morning as on a hot afternoon.

blocks.title: Over-fermented dough
blocks.text: If dough smells strongly of alcohol, has collapsed, or feels slack and tears easily, it has over-fermented. The bread will spread, be pale and taste sour. Next time use cooler water, less yeast or a shorter rise. Do not try to fix it by adding more flour.

takeaways: Yeast works best at about 24 to 27 C and dies around 60 C.
Active dry is about 1.25 times instant; fresh about 2.5 to 3 times.
Water temperature = target x 3 minus room, flour and friction.
Judge bulk fermentation by the dough, not only the clock.

activity.title: Hit your dough temperature
steps: Measure your room and flour temperature with a probe thermometer.
Calculate the water temperature for a 25 C dough (estimate friction at 3 C by hand).
Mix a simple lean dough and measure its final temperature.
Record bulk fermentation time and a photo of the risen dough in a marked container.
activity.evidence: Your calculation, final dough temperature, bulk time and the before and after container photos.

lessons.title: Dividing, shaping, proofing and scoring
objectives: Divide dough accurately by weight and allow for bake loss
Pre-shape and final shape rounds, batards and tin loaves with good surface tension
Use the poke test to judge proofing
Score and steam loaves for a good rise and crust

blocks.text: Two bakers can use the same dough and get very different loaves. The difference is in the hands: how evenly they divide, how much tension they build when shaping, how well they judge proofing, and how cleanly they score. These are the skills that make bread look professional on a shop shelf.

blocks.name: baguette-bread
blocks.caption: Clean, confident scoring lets the loaf open in a controlled way in the oven.

blocks.text: Divide by weight

Always divide with a bench scraper and a scale, never by eye. Cut, do not tear, and use as few pieces per portion as possible. Remember that bread loses weight in the oven as water evaporates. Bake loss is often around 10 to 15% depending on size, shape and bake time, so weigh a few baked loaves from your own oven to know your figure.

blocks.title: Worked example: dividing for a shop order
blocks.context: For example, Musa in Jos supplies a supermarket with 400 g baked tin loaves. His own tests show a bake loss of about 12%.
steps: Dough weight per loaf: 400 / (1 - 0.12) = 400 / 0.88 = about 455 g.
His dough batch is 5,000 g. 5,000 / 455 = 10.99, so 10 full loaves.
10 x 455 = 4,550 g, leaving 450 g, just short of an eleventh loaf.
He adds about 5 g of dough to the batch (5,005 g) next time so that 11 x 455 = 5,005 g, giving eleven loaves with no leftover.
blocks.result: Every loaf now meets the 400 g label weight after baking, and Musa gets an extra loaf per batch from a tiny adjustment.

blocks.text: Pre-shape and rest
